## Agent Benchmarks Changed the Evidence Standard

Agent benchmarks changed the object being measured. The most influential benchmarks of this period did not mainly test multi-agent coordination. They asked whether a harnessed agent could browse, use tools, operate software, modify repositories, follow policies, interact with users, and leave the external world in the intended state. Web benchmarks tested browser state and functional task completion [@mind2web; @webarena; @webvoyager; @visualwebarena; @browsergym]. GUI, mobile, and social benchmarks tested perception, interaction, device state, and social state [@sotopia; @osworld; @androidworld]. Assistant and API benchmarks tested tool use, user interaction, policy following, and workplace tasks [@agentbench; @agentboard; @gaia; @workarena; @taubench; @agentcompany]. Coding benchmarks tested whether agents could modify real repositories and satisfy tests rather than merely generate snippets [@swebench]. The important historical point is not that many benchmarks appeared. It is that they made agent failure observable. @fig-agentbench is one representative example of this shift from answer generation to interactive environment evaluation.

![AgentBench evaluation architecture with agent servers, task servers, and an evaluation client that coordinates assignments across interactive environments. The measured object is not a single answer but a loop of planning, action, observation, and task completion. Reproduced from @agentbench.](figures/agentbench-framework.png){#fig-agentbench width=92% fig-alt="AgentBench framework diagram showing an LLM agent interacting with multiple evaluation environments through actions and observations."}

The target changed. The question was no longer whether an agent could produce a plausible answer in one response. It was whether it could maintain state, use tools, recover from errors, inspect evidence, satisfy hidden constraints, and know when it was done. Across these settings, the dominant single-agent failures were not exotic reasoning mistakes. They were operational failures: losing task state, misreading observations, choosing invalid actions, exploring weakly, stopping too early, repeating steps, over-trusting partial evidence, and failing to verify completion. WebArena highlighted early stopping, weak exploration, observation bias, and repeated invalid actions; OSWorld highlighted GUI grounding and app-specific operational knowledge; tau-bench made repeated-trial reliability visible through pass^k rather than a single success rate [@webarena; @osworld; @taubench].

The original papers reported large early gaps. WebArena reported a best GPT-4-based baseline of 14.41% success versus 78.24% for humans; VisualWebArena reported GPT-4V-based variants at 15.05-16.37% versus 88.70% for humans; OSWorld reported a best model setting of 12.24% versus 72.36% for humans; GAIA reported GPT-4 with plugins around 15% versus about 92% for humans [@webarena; @visualwebarena; @osworld; @gaia]. Later benchmarks broadened the same lesson: AndroidWorld reported GPT-4 Turbo M3A at 30.6% versus 80.0% for humans, and TheAgentCompany reported its best baseline completing 30.3% of full workplace tasks, or 39.3% with partial credit [@androidworld; @agentcompany]. These numbers should not be treated as current capability limits, because model versions, prompts, tool APIs, and harnesses change quickly. They are evidence for the historical point: realistic tool-use evaluation exposed a large gap between fluent interaction and reliable task completion.

This mattered for multi-agent research because teams inherit the weaknesses of their workers. A second agent can search another branch, check a claim, or use a different tool, but it can also inherit a bad premise, summarize away critical state, duplicate an invalid plan, trust another agent's unfinished work, or terminate around a false consensus. Once tasks involve long horizons and external state, a multi-agent system must justify its coordination overhead. It must show that extra agents add something more than extra calls. It must survive cost accounting, stronger baselines, repeated trials, and realistic validators. *AI Agents That Matter* [@aiagentsmatter] made this general point for agent benchmarks: downstream usefulness requires cost-controlled comparisons, shortcut-resistant evaluation, standardized reporting, and metrics aligned with actual task value. A multi-agent result should therefore beat at least three controls when they are relevant: a budget-matched single agent, independent sampling or voting, and a strong fixed workflow or agentless pipeline.

The same logic is now appearing inside multi-agent evaluation itself. MultiAgentBench and Collab-Overcooked make collaboration and competition explicit objects of measurement rather than assuming they are present because agents communicate [@multiagentbench; @collabovercooked]. AgentsNet tests whether networks of language agents can coordinate through local message passing on distributed graph tasks, including settings where larger graphs degrade performance sharply [@agentsnet]. MASLab addresses another problem: comparisons across multi-agent methods are fragile when implementations, prompts, tool wrappers, and evaluation protocols differ; in its MATH audit, evaluator choice can move reported AgentVerse performance from 79.0 to 25.6 [@maslab]. Together, these papers push the field toward a review standard that asks what kind of evidence each system provides. Does it show which single-agent failure the team is meant to repair? Does it isolate a multi-agent mechanism? Does it compare against budget-matched single-agent, sampling, and workflow baselines? Does it report tokens, dollars, latency, and repeated-run variance? Does it inspect traces rather than only final scores? Does it evaluate intermediate artifacts and degradation over time?

Executable environments changed the standard of evidence. The next question was what those measurements revealed about multi-agent claims.
